{{short description|Theorem in abstract algebra}}
The '''Latimer–MacDuffee theorem''' is a [[theorem]] in [[abstract algebra]], a branch of [[mathematics]]. 
It is named after [[Claiborne Latimer]] and [[Cyrus Colton MacDuffee]], who published it in 1933.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Latimer | first1 = Claiborne G. | author1-link = Claiborne Latimer
 | last2 = MacDuffee | first2 = C. C. | author2-link = Cyrus Colton MacDuffee
 | doi = 10.2307/1968204
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Annals of Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1503108
 | pages = 313–316
 | series = Second Series
 | title = A correspondence between classes of ideals and classes of matrices
 | volume = 34
 | year = 1933| jstor = 1968204 }}.</ref> Significant contributions to its theory were made later by [[Olga Taussky-Todd]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Hanlon | first = Phil
 | author-link = Philip J. Hanlon
 | doi = 10.1016/S0024-3795(98)10006-X
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Linear Algebra and Its Applications
 | mr = 1642834
 | pages = 21–37
 | title = To the Latimer-Macduffee theorem and beyond!
 | volume = 280
 | year = 1998| doi-access = 
 }}.</ref>

Let <math>f</math> be a [[monic polynomial|monic]], [[irreducible polynomial]] of degree <math>n</math>.  The Latimer–MacDuffee theorem gives a [[Bijection|one-to-one correspondence]] between <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-[[matrix similarity|similarity classes]] of <math>n\times n</math> [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] with [[characteristic polynomial]] <math>f</math> and the [[ideal class]]es in the [[Order (ring theory)|order]]

:<math>\mathbb{Z}[x]/(f(x)). </math>

where ideals are considered equivalent if they are equal up to an overall (nonzero) rational scalar multiple. (Note that this order need not be the full ring of integers, so nonzero ideals need not be invertible.)  Since an order in a number field has only finitely many ideal classes (even if it is not the maximal order, and we mean here ideals classes for all nonzero ideals, not just the invertible ones), it follows that there are only finitely many [[conjugacy class]]es of matrices over the integers with characteristic polynomial <math>f(x)</math>.
